title: Cleaning quotes
objectives: Filter out stale, crossed and zero-bid quotes.
Drop quotes whose spread is too wide relative to their mid.

screens.title: Quotes you would not trust

screens.title: Four rules
screens.prose: Written as rules, a quote is kept when its bid is positive, its bid is at most its ask, it is at most 30 minutes old, and its **relative spread** $(a - b)/m$ is below 0.5, where $m$ is the mid.
screens.question: What is the relative spread of the six-month 105 call, 4.48 / 7.60?

hints.text: Spread first, then mid.
The spread is $7.60 - 4.48 = 3.12$ and the mid is 6.04.

feedback.correct: 0.517: over the 0.5 cut, so it is dropped.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Divide the spread by the mid.

byKey.abs: You stopped at ask minus bid. Divide by the mid to make it relative.
byKey.bid: You divided by the bid. The rule divides by the mid, 6.04.
byKey.ask: You divided by the ask. The rule divides by the mid, 6.04.

explain.text: The spread, £3.12, is 0.517 of the mid, £6.04. That is over the 0.5 cut, so the rule drops it. Its neighbours at six months have relative spreads near 0.06.

screens.title: Does the order matter?
screens.prose: Applied in this order to the 130 quotes of `make_chain()`, the rules drop 15, 2, 2 and 9 rows, leaving 102. A zero-bid quote has mid $a/2$, so its relative spread is $a/(a/2) = 2$.
screens.question: Apply the wide-spread rule first instead. How many rows does it drop?

widget.label: Rows dropped by the wide rule
widget.accept: 24 exactly: the 9 wide quotes plus all 15 zero bids

hints.text: Which other rows have a relative spread of at least 0.5?
Every zero-bid quote has relative spread 2.

feedback.correct: 24: the wide rule now also catches every zero bid.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Count the wide quotes plus any others with a relative spread of 0.5 or more.

byKey.same: You kept the count from the first order. Every zero bid also fails the spread rule, since its relative spread is 2.
byKey.all: Crossed and stale quotes pass the spread rule: a crossed spread is negative. Only zero bids join the wide ones.

explain.text: First, the wide rule drops 24 rows and the zero-bid rule then finds none. The kept set is the same 102, as a row survives only if it passes all four. Only the labels move, so log each row's first failing reason in a fixed order.

screens.title: A locked market
screens.prose: A quote whose bid equals its ask is **locked**: a buyer and a seller agree on the price but have not yet traded. Here is one, fresh, on the three-month 105 call.
screens.question: Do our four rules keep it?

options.text: Yes: the bid is positive and at most the ask, and the spread is 0
No: it fails the bid-at-most-ask rule
options.why: You tested bid below ask. The rule is bid at most ask, and 2.15 ≤ 2.15 holds; crossed means bid above ask.

options.text: No: a zero spread is suspicious, so the spread rule drops it
options.why: The spread rule drops wide quotes. A zero spread is the tightest possible.

hints.text: Test each rule on 2.15 / 2.15.
All four rules pass, so the quote stays.

feedback.correct: Kept: a locked quote is a real price.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Test each of the four rules in turn.

explain.text: Bid 2.15 is positive and at most the ask, the quote is fresh, and its relative spread is 0. All four rules pass. In code that is `bid <= ask`, not `bid < ask`.

screens.title: Filling a zero bid
screens.prose: A colleague hates losing rows. He fills every zero bid with £0.01 and keeps the quote. Take the three-month 95 call, quoted 0.00 / 7.97. Its lower bound is $Se^{-qT} - Ke^{-rT} = \text{£}5.93$.
screens.question: Is his filled quote a price we can fit a volatility to?

options.text: Yes: with the gap filled it is a quote like any other
options.why: You trusted the invented bid. Its mid, £3.99, is below the lower bound of £5.93, where no volatility exists.

options.text: No: its mid, £3.99, is below the lower bound, so no volatility fits
Yes, if we use the ask, £7.97, as the price
options.why: The ask alone is only an upper limit on value. Treating it as the price biases every one-sided quote upwards.

options.text: Yes: the spread rule will catch it anyway
options.why: It would here, with relative spread near 2. But a filled wing quote such as 0.01 / 0.03 passes the spread rule and fakes a vol.

hints.text: Work out the filled mid and compare it with the bound.
£3.99 is below £5.93, so no volatility prices it.

feedback.correct: The filled mid lies below the lower bound: no vol fits.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Compute the filled mid and set it against £5.93.

byKey.keep: You kept a quote with an invented bid. The £0.01 is made up, so its mid of £3.99 is half the ask, not a price.

explain.text: The £0.01 is invented, so the mid is just half the ask, £3.99. Here that lands below the lower bound, where no volatility exists. In the wings it fakes a low vol instead, so drop zero bids and count them in the log.

screens.title: The cleaning mask
screens.prose:
Each rule you applied is a test on one row, so the four combine with *and*: keep iff $b > 0$, $b \le a$, $\text{age} \le 30$ and $(a - b)/m < 0.5$.

```python
m = (df["bid"] + df["ask"]) / 2
keep = ((df["bid"] > 0) & (df["bid"] <= df["ask"])
        & (df["age_min"] <= 30)
        & ((df["ask"] - df["bid"]) / m < 0.5))
```
screens.question: Which test keeps the locked quote 2.15 / 2.15 but drops 2.20 / 2.15?

options.why: That drops the locked quote too, since 2.15 < 2.15 is false.
That drops the locked quote and keeps the crossed one.
That keeps only locked and crossed quotes: the opposite of what we want.

feedback.correct: `<=` keeps equality and drops bid above ask.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Try both quotes in each test.

explain.text: `bid <= ask` is true for 2.15 / 2.15 and false for 2.20 / 2.15. The mask is a Series of booleans, so `df[keep]` keeps the rows that pass all four.

widget.solution:
import pandas as pd

# make_chain() is loaded as chain.

def clean_quotes(df, max_age_min=30, max_rel_spread=0.5):
    """Keep two-sided, uncrossed, fresh, tight quotes."""
    m = (df["bid"] + df["ask"]) / 2
    keep = ((df["bid"] > 0) & (df["bid"] <= df["ask"])
            & (df["age_min"] <= max_age_min)
            & ((df["ask"] - df["bid"]) / m < max_rel_spread))
    return df[keep].reset_index(drop=True)
widget.how: `make_chain()` is loaded as `chain`, and `quotes(rows)` builds a hand-made frame from rows of `[T, strike, type, bid, ask, volume, age_min]`. Check runs 11 hidden tests, one per rule and a locked quote, then row counts on the chain, all compared exactly. The first run loads numpy and pandas, which can take ten seconds or more.

hints.text: Build one boolean Series with `&`, each test in brackets.
The age test uses the argument: `df["age_min"] <= max_age_min`.
Then `return df[keep].reset_index(drop=True)`.

feedback.correct: 102 of 130 survive, with a fresh index.
feedback.generic: Some tests failed. Check each rule's comparison, the arguments and the reset index.

explain.text: Each comparison gives a boolean Series and `&` combines them row by row. Brackets matter, because `&` binds tighter than `<=`. `reset_index(drop=True)` numbers the survivors from 0 without keeping the old index as a column.

widget.solution:
import pandas as pd

# make_chain() is loaded as chain.

def drop_report(df, max_age_min=30, max_rel_spread=0.5):
    """Rows dropped per reason, each under its first failing rule."""
    m = (df["bid"] + df["ask"]) / 2
    rules = [("zero_bid", df["bid"] <= 0),
             ("crossed", df["bid"] > df["ask"]),
             ("stale", df["age_min"] > max_age_min),
             ("wide", (df["ask"] - df["bid"]) / m >= max_rel_spread)]
    left = pd.Series(True, index=df.index)   # not yet dropped
    report = {}
    for name, bad in rules:
        report[name] = int((left & bad).sum())
        left = left & ~bad
    report["kept"] = int(left.sum())
    return report
widget.how: `make_chain()` is loaded as `chain`, and `quotes(rows)` builds a hand-made frame. Check runs 7 hidden tests; each dict must match exactly, keys in order. The first run loads numpy and pandas, which can take ten seconds or more.

hints.text: A row counts under a rule only if no earlier rule dropped it.
`left & bad` marks rows still in play that fail this rule.
`report[name] = int((left & bad).sum())`, then `left = left & ~bad`.

feedback.correct: Every row counted once, under its first failing rule.
feedback.generic: Some tests failed. Count only rows still in play, then remove them.

explain.text: `left` starts all true and loses each rule's failures in turn. So a zero-bid quote that is also wide counts once, as a zero bid. `int(...)` turns NumPy counts into plain integers for the note.

screens.title: A stale quote in a book
screens.prose: A vol desk logs every dropped quote. Suppose the stale one-year 95 call had slipped through. It was set when the share stood at £102, so at today's £100 it implies 26.7% instead of 22.7%. The desk is short 500 of these calls, with vega £34.57 per contract per vol point.
screens.question: Marked on that surface, how much does the short book appear to lose?

hints.text: Vega converts vol points to pounds.
Each contract loses about $34.57 \times 4.03$.
Multiply by 500 contracts.

feedback.correct: About £69,700 of loss that is not real.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Multiply vega by the vol gap and by the number of contracts.

byKey.one: That is one contract. The book is short 500.
byKey.per-share: You used vega per share. The £34.57 already covers the 100 shares of a contract.

explain.text: One stale quote moves the 95 vol by 4 points and marks the book down about £69,700. Its Greeks shift too, so the hedges would be wrong. That is why a desk logs every quote it drops or keeps.

ideas: Keep a quote when its bid is positive, its bid is at most its ask, it is at most 30 minutes old, and its relative spread is below 0.5. On `make_chain()` that keeps 102 of 130.
The kept set does not depend on the order of the rules; the reason logged for each dropped row does. Log it in a fixed order.
Never invent a bid. A zero bid, a crossed quote or a stale quote is dropped and counted, not repaired.
